# Dfns

[Glyph index](glyphs.qmd)

A dfn is a function written in braces. `⍵` is its right argument, and `⍺` is its left argument.

```bpl
{⍵×2}3             ⍝ 6
2{⍺+⍵}3            ⍝ 5
```

## Statements

A dfn holds statements, separated by `⋄` or line breaks. Every statement runs in order. The last statement gives the result, and the values of earlier statements are discarded.

```bpl
{x←⍵+1 ⋄ x×2}3     ⍝ 8
{1 ⋄ 2}0           ⍝ 2
```

A statement can run only for its side effect. Here the Each adds to `s`, and the last statement returns `s`.

```bpl
{s←0 ⋄ {s+←⍵}¨⍵ ⋄ s}1 2 3   ⍝ 6
```

A final assignment returns its value without displaying it.

```bpl
{x←⍵+1}3           ⍝ 4
```

## Scope

Names follow lexical scope. Plain assignment creates a name local to the dfn. Modified assignment, such as `+←`, updates the nearest existing binding, which can belong to an enclosing dfn or to the top level.

```bpl
aa←3 ⋄ bob←{aa+←⍵ ⋄ aa} ⋄ bob 5   ⍝ 8
{gg←1 ⋄ {gg←⍵}¨⍳⍵ ⋄ gg}5          ⍝ 1
```

## Bodies and predicates

`;` separates a dfn's bodies. A [predicate](glyphs/question.qmd) `C?` tests `C`, which must be a Boolean singleton. When `C` is true, the rest of the body runs. When it is false, the dfn moves on to its next body.

```bpl
{⍵<0?-⍵;⍵}¯3                             ⍝ 3
{⍵<0?a←-⍵ ⋄ a×2;⍵}¯3                     ⍝ 6
{a←⍵ ⋄ a>9?"big";a>0?"small";"none"}5   ⍝ "small"
```

Statements before a predicate run first. All the bodies share one scope. For example, a name assigned in one body is visible in later bodies. Every body but the last needs a predicate. If every predicate fails, the call is a `DOMAIN` error.

An empty body returns no result. Examples are `{}` and the first body of `{⍵≡0?;⍵}`, which ends right after its predicate.

## Arguments

In a call with one argument, `⍺` is absent. An expression that uses an absent `⍺` is evaluated as if `⍺` weren't there. For example, `⍺ f ⍵` calls `f` with one argument, `f ⍺` is itself absent, and `[⍺ ⍵]` is `[⍵]`. One dfn can therefore serve both cases. Any other use, such as `x←⍺` or `⍺` as an operand, is a `VALUE` error.

```bpl
{⍺-⍵}3             ⍝ ¯3
10{⍺-⍵}3           ⍝ 7
{(2×⍺)-⍵}3         ⍝ ¯3
{[⍺ ⍵]}3           ⍝ [3]
```

`⍺←` gives `⍺` a [default](glyphs/alpha.qmd). The assignment runs only when `⍺` is absent.

```bpl
{⍺←10 ⋄ ⍺-⍵}3      ⍝ 7
2{⍺←10 ⋄ ⍺-⍵}3     ⍝ ¯1
```

[Valences](glyphs/valences.qmd) `⊘` joins a monadic function and a dyadic function into one.

## Recursion

[`∇`](glyphs/del.qmd) calls the current dfn. Tail calls reuse execution frames.

```bpl
{⍵=0?1;⍵×∇⍵-1}5    ⍝ 120
```

## Operators

`⍶` is a dfn's left operand, and `⍹` is its right operand. A dfn that uses `⍶` is a monadic operator, and a dfn that uses `⍹` is a dyadic operator. [`⍢`](glyphs/del-diaeresis.qmd) refers to the current operator, for recursion with new operands.

```bpl
twice←{⍶ ⍶ ⍵} ⋄ (-twice)3   ⍝ 3
2 (+{⍺ ⍶ ⍹ ⍵}-) 3            ⍝ ¯1
```

## Error guards

An [error guard](glyphs/error-guard.qmd) `codes::handler` catches matching errors in the statements after it, including those in later bodies. The handler's value becomes the result.

```bpl
{11::0 ⋄ ÷⍵}"a"    ⍝ 0
```

## Design

BPL's dfns come from Dyalog APL, with three rules from BQN's [blocks](https://mlochbaum.github.io/BQN/doc/block.html). Every statement runs, and the last gives the result. Predicates choose between bodies separated by `;`. A left argument that isn't given drops out of the expression, as BQN's `𝕨` does.

In Dyalog APL, a statement that isn't an assignment returns at once, skipping the statements after it. Running a statement only for its side effect needs a workaround.

BPL leaves out two BQN features that Marshall Lochbaum's [five-year review of BQN's design](https://mlochbaum.github.io/BQN/commentary/fiveyears.html) criticises. BPL doesn't choose a body by argument count, which the review calls useless. Valences covers that case. BPL also has no block headers, which the review finds more complex than they need to be. The review reports that BQN's rule for `𝕨` has held up, and that ambivalent code is easier to write with it than with tacit combinators.

The review would rather not decide a block's kind from special names in its body. BPL keeps that rule. Braces always define a function or an operator. A body that uses `⍶` or `⍹` defines an operator, and any other body defines a function.

Unlike a BQN block, a dfn keeps one scope across its bodies, as Dyalog APL's guards do.
